#1025. Controversial kinship: From colonial rule to the Holocaust?

Hitler once called Eastern Europe "Germany's India." A new exhibition examines the links between colonialism and Nazism, and the bitter debate over where comparisons illuminate history and where they fall short.

Racial hierarchy, dehumanization, concentration camps, settler expansion in the name of "living space," collective punishment and mass violence: At first glance, the continuities between colonial and Nazi violence appear obvious. In 1941, Nazi dictator Adolf Hitler himself compared Eastern Europe to "Germany's India" after the British colonial model, declaring that "like the English, we shall rule this empire with a handful of men."

But the extent to which Nazism was shaped by the age of empire and whether the two systems of violence can even be compared remains the subject of intense debate.

This is particularly true in Germany, where the fear is often expressed that any comparison risks relativizing or minimizing Nazi crimes, and particularly the Holocaust. Others have argued that the intense focus on the Nazi era has, at least in part, come at the expense of a meaningful reckoning with Germany's colonial history.

"I do think this is nonsense," says Stephan Malinowski, a Professor of Modern European History at the University of Edinburgh. "If it were true, then all other colonial countries who are not discussing the Holocaust, like Great Britain for example, or France or Spain or Portugal, they would then supposedly be very, very attentive to colonial crimes and to colonial history, which it seems to me is not the case."

"Controversial Kinship: Colonial and National Socialist Violence," a new exhibition at the German Historical Museum in Berlin curated by Malinowski, does not aim to settle the debate but to tell its story.

The exhibition begins with a hippopotamus-hide whip used in African colonies displayed alongside a canister of Zyklon B, the poison used in Nazi gas chambers. The juxtaposition highlights the contrast between colonial violence and the industrialized mass murder of the Holocaust.

Yet it also points to connections: Whips were used in Nazi concentration camps, while Fascist Italy deployed chemical weapons against civilians and soldiers during its invasion of Ethiopia (then Abyssinia) in 1935-36.

In the 1930s, anti-colonial thinkers from India to the Caribbean argued that colonialism and fascism were two sides of the same coin. "There is nothing new or original about the blustering exploits of Hitler and Mussolini," observed the Trinidadian journalist and Pan-Africanist George Padmore in 1938. "They have all been used before by the British in their efforts to obtain the subjection of less powerfully armed and more industrially backward people."

European colonial rule was marked by the ruthless exploitation of people and resources, often enforced through extreme violence. In "The Origins of Totalitarianism" (1951), German-American philosopher Hannah Arendt argued that colonial territories served as laboratories for racial ideologies and practices of domination that could be applied beyond the legal constraints of Europe. Arendt described how these later "boomeranged" back into Europe and helped shape totalitarian politics in distinct and unprecedented form.

The Congo Free State, King Leopold II of Belgium's private colony from 1885 to 1908, became notorious for its extreme brutality, as colonial authorities used executions, amputations and sexual violence to ensure rubber production quotas were met.

Forced labor was also central to Nazi rule, with millions of Poles, Ukrainians, Russians and others from the Soviet Union, and Jews, subjected to exploitation and "Vernichtung durch Arbeit" ("extermination through work"). Within a few years, the regime mobilized around 13 to 14 million forced laborers, a scale comparable to the transatlantic slave trade over more than three centuries. The Nazis sought to extract value from their victims at every stage, confiscating their property, exploiting their labor, and even harvesting gold teeth and hair from the dead.

While racism underpinned both colonial empires and Nazism, Malinowski says the goals were different. The colonial powers tended to present assimilation as a path to advancement, forcing colonized people to adopt European culture, serve imperial interests, and suggesting that a select, educated few could gain opportunities, for example at elite institutions such as Oxford or Cambridge. "This is definitely not something that the Nazi regime is offering to Poles or to Russians or let alone to Jews," added Malinowski.

"In terms of violence, colonial violence was just as extreme as Nazi violence. But Nazi violence was annihilatory and exterminatory compared to colonial violence in the colonies," says Edward Kissi, a historian at the School of Interdisciplinary Global Studies at the University of South Florida. He points to the example of how, unlike European colonial powers in Africa, the Nazis pursued the elimination of Black-Germans or peoples of African descent in Germany through forced sterilization. "Even in racism, colonial color-based racism and colonial anti-Jewish sentiments were fundamentally different from what the Nazis pursued."

On October 2, 1904, German General Lothar von Trotha issued the "Vernichtungsbefehl" ("extermination order") following the Herero uprising in German South West Africa (present-day Namibia). Historians generally attribute the order to a combination of racial ideology, a desire to terrorize the population into submission, and efforts to secure colonial control over land, labor and resources. Between 1904 and 1908, an estimated 60,000 to 80,000 Herero (around 80% of the population) and 10,000 (around half the population) Nama died.

One area where the exhibition draws no direct parallel is the industrialized killing carried out in Nazi death camps such as Belzec, Sobibor, Treblinka, and Auschwitz-Birkenau. "Where the two things really diverge is the Holocaust and is the systematic mass murder of the European Jews and it's murder for the very purpose of murder," explains Malinowski. The deportation of around 1,800 Jews from the Greek islands of Rhodes and Kos in July 1944 illustrates how Nazi persecution often defied military or economic logic. Even after the war was effectively lost, the community was transported to Auschwitz, where most were murdered immediately upon arrival.

The issue of the "singularity" of the Holocaust came to the fore during the 1980s "Historikerstreit" ("historians' dispute"). Historian Ernst Nolte argued that Nazism should be understood in the wider context of 20th-century political violence, and as a response to Bolshevik terror in particular. Critics accused him of downplaying German responsibility for Nazi crimes.

Since 2020, a renewed debate dubbed the "Historikerstreit 2.0" has focused on whether the Holocaust should be viewed as a unique reference point in German memory culture or be understood alongside the histories of colonialism, racism and empire. The dispute now is less about the legitimacy of comparison than about its implications.

The mass murder of tens of thousands of the Herero and Nama during four years of German colonial rule is now regarded as the first genocide of the 20th-century. But in 2016, Nama representatives walked out of talks after Germany's chief negotiator said what happened was "incomparable" to the Holocaust. The German government has since recognized the events as genocide "from today's perspective," but it has not yet accepted legal liability or agreed to pay formal reparations.

Martinican intellectual Aime Cesaire argued in "Discourse on Colonialism" (1950) that Europe condemned under Nazism forms of violence it had long accepted in its colonies. More than 70 years later, the exhibition opens amid renewed debates over the definition of settler colonialism and genocide, and the meaning of "never again," sharpened by Nicaragua's case against Germany at the International Court of Justice over Germany's support for Israel during the war in Gaza and its alleged failure to uphold its obligations under the Genocide Convention to prevent genocide.

These tensions are reflected in visitors' comments in the exhibition's epilogue, even though the exhibition itself does not address Israel or Palestine beyond a reference to Mohammed Amin al-Husseini, appointed Grand Mufti of Jerusalem in 1921.

Germany has unequivocally accepted responsibility for the Holocaust, which is front and center of the country's culture of remembrance.  However, Kissi likens Germany's apparent reluctance to reckon with its colonial history to debates in the US over slavery, in Cambodia over the Khmer Rouge, and in Turkey over the Armenian genocide. According to him, Germany's contemporary identity cannot be fully understood without examining its colonial history and the ways the Nazis appropriated and transformed aspects of that legacy.

"I think Germans and all other human beings who have experienced violent pasts and difficult pasts should be very careful not to delink or dissociate those facts from their present," Kissi said. "These are historical patterns. It is better to deal with these historical patterns and discomforts than to just fight them and then say this has absolutely nothing to do with German national identity."

"Controversial Kinship: Colonial and National Socialist Violence" is on show at the German Historical Museum until April 11, 2027.

#1021. How the Glazers REALLY feel about Man United: IAN HERBERT reveals the family split over selling club, their regrets over Sir Jim Ratcliffe 'mistake' and Richard Arnold exit... and their missed chance to 'cash out'

Published: 12:00 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 12:03 EST, 24 November 2026

An Amazon Prime documentary series about the Glazers' Tampa Bay Buccaneers American football team paints a revealing picture of the billionaire family coalescing around a sport they actually love. It feels a very long way from Manchester United, the club they have taken down to the depths.

All six children of Malcolm Glazer, the man who built the business empire and bought United in 2005, share stories of their childhood NFL obsession. Darcie Glazer Kassewitz, sister to five Glazer brothers, relates how, on the day before they all went to a Miami Dolphins game, her brothers would be in the basement with bedsheets and paint creating huge banners.

Sometimes playing ‘knee football’ down there. Or competing in what they called the ‘BYFL’ – the ‘back-yard football league’ they set up among themselves and neighbours. ‘They all loved sports,’ says their mother, Linda.

Of course, the British form of football doesn’t feature.

This homespun scene contrasts with the family’s current dismay about the chaos created at Manchester United, which has led to renewed discussion among several of the siblings about selling off some, or all, of their shareholding.

Most of the siblings consider selling a minority share to Sir Jim Ratcliffe to have been a mistake, according to a source with a social connection to the Glazers. Though there is not a sense of how the family feel about individual Ratcliffe appointees, they are thought to rue the departure of Richard Arnold – former United commercial director and chief executive, whose part working on dozens of commercial deals saw him oversee around £4billion of revenue.

Manchester United's dismal form this season hasn't gone unnoticed by their owners in the United States, some of whom have discussed cashing in on their shareholding

American football - and their team the Tampa Bay Buccaneers - is the Glazers' true love. Joel Glazer led the celebrations when they won the Super Bowl in 2021

The Glazers have been ‘surprised’ at the loss of other influential senior staff, according to the source.

Arnold saw the writing on the wall before Ratcliffe and Ineos arrived. He personally negotiated his own exit with the Glazers. But they were then unable to prevent other departures which have been detrimental to the club, according to sources with no Glazer connection who have worked with United.

Those lost include the highly respected Victoria Timpson, United's former 'CEO of Alliances and Partnerships', who struck the Snapdragon and Teamviewer shirt sponsorship deal, but left in December 2024.

Florence Lafaye, former United commercial director, briefly took over Timpson’s responsibilities but also left to join Timpson in establishing the commercial agency Altius8, which was soon hired by Tottenham Hotspur.

Joel, Avram and Bryan Glazer are the three siblings thought to relish owning United – a calling card they have used at, among other settings, the Davos World Economic Forum, where United were the only football club to take a pavilion in the past.

Joel, whose 10.7 per cent shareholding is the biggest of the six siblings, was often seen as a man of interference before Ratcliffe’s arrival, pushing for higher fees when executive vice chairman Ed Woodward or others were trying to negotiate a transfer sale.

But the interest in United of Kevin, Ed and Darcie is far less certain, even though all six sit on the United board and Darcie holds the second largest share at 9.71 per cent.

The six collectively wanted to test the water for a sale after seeing US financier Todd Boehly pay £4.25billion for Chelsea in 2022. They formed the impression that United could sell for twice that much.

The sale of a share to Ratcliffe was held up by the six failing to agree on whether to sell up entirely or just let go of the football side of the business.

Most of the Glazer siblings consider selling a minority share of Manchester United to Sir Jim Ratcliffe to have been a mistake

The interest in Manchester United of Kevin, Ed and Darcie Glazer (pictured) is far from certain, even though all six sit on the United board

An extensive report about United by Bloomberg last week suggested some individual family members were considering the sale of more of their shareholding and hoping to convince others among the six to join them.

The unexpected summer purchase of a stake in Liverpool by a Jeff Bezos-led consortium had caught several members of the family ‘off guard’, leaving some of the six feeling they had missed an opportunity to cash out. That deal has a potential takeover clause which could value Liverpool at £5.3bn.

The original plan was that Ratcliffe would ultimately buy the rest of United for £4bn, but since buying into the club, his chemicals business has been hit by a prolonged industrial downturn, collapsing profitability and high energy costs.

The Ineos Industries division recorded a £1.84bn pre-tax loss in 2025, his chemicals empire is carrying more than £10bn of net debt and he has been exiting from most of his sports interests.

The Glazers have the power, under the terms of their deal with Ratcliffe, to sell the club outright and force him to sell his stake. Another option would be to divest themselves of a small slice of their 48.9 per cent stake. But the current uncertainty about the future landscape of the Premier League created by the Manchester City case, with a slew of possible legal cases in its wake, is impacting on outside investment in top-flight clubs.

The family may have to sit tight and hope the recovery of the club’s fortunes, allied to plans for a new £2bn stadium, will take the club’s value closer to the £6bn that the six would be likely to agree on as an exit figure. They could tap into the bond market as Barcelona did to finance their $1.5bn upgrade of Camp Nou, or look to private equity funds, who would want a major pay-back when the stadium is built.

But for the first time through their 21 years as owners, United face the frightening predicament of relegation – bringing, for example, a £5.7million-a-year TV deal in the Championship compared with the £191.5m in Premier League income banked last season.

With new Premier League Squad Cost Ratio rules allowing the club to spend 85 per cent of last year’s £677.6m revenue on players and £160m in the club’s rotating credit facility, there is money.

Multiple sources say the Glazers stepped in to ensure Mauricio Pochettino’s appointment – something United deny

The Glazer family are thought to rue the departure of Richard Arnold (pictured), the club's former commercial director and chief executive

Multiple sources say the Glazers stepped in to ensure Mauricio Pochettino’s appointment – something United deny. But the source close to the family also believes they will now continue to present a greater challenge to what many see as Ratcliffe’s running down of the United operation.

The Bloomberg report showed how Ratcliffe’s 300 job cuts had focused heavily on commercial, media and administrative divisions, which former employees said had eroded relations with corporate partners and caused a deterioration in the level of service.

A former executive described how long-standing sponsors, accustomed to receiving complimentary autographed merchandise, were told they should expect to pay shipping fees for signed memorabilia. ‘Penny wise, pound foolish,’ the executive said. This was certainly not the Glazer way under Woodward and Arnold, who built that side of the operation.

The Glazers are 47th in the Forbes list of most wealthy US families and the Amazon Tampa Bay Bucs series reveals an innate obsession with the financial bottom line and making profit. ‘My father didn’t give a damn about what anybody else thought,’ Ed Glazer tells the film-makers. ‘He would always say, “Why can’t we do this?”. We could look at anything as long as the numbers made sense.’

It’s hard to believe that Ratcliffe, a man desperately trying to preserve his own business, is going to get in the way of the Glazers seeking ways to preserve the long-neglected asset which is now staring into the abyss.

#1020. Germany slips in climate protection rankings as other countries make gains

Record renewable energy growth is driving climate progress in some countries, but Germany and many major emitters are falling behind.

Germany has slipped down the climate action ranking for the third consecutive year, with the former green leader now being outperformed by Brazil, Colombia and Romania.

In its worst performance since 2019, the country fell to place 25 and received a "medium" rating overall on the yearly Climate Change Performance Index (CCPI), which assesses efforts to curb global warming in 64 countries plus the European Union.

Still, "a number of countries have been making good progress for years," said Jan Burck, CCPI lead author, in a statement. Denmark is leading the way across all four categories assessed — energy use, greenhouse gas emissions, renewable energy and national climate policy. A total of 15 states, including Lithuania, Chile, and Morocco, received an overall "high" rating, which is two more than last year.

The European Union also moved up a spot, while Hungary jumped 21 places after the ousting of former prime minister Viktor Orban's government, which had repeatedly vetoed EU climate plans, dismissing them as a "utopian fantasy."

The top three positions on the CCPI remained vacant again this year, as no country has yet done enough to meet global climate goals aimed at preventing worsening weather extremes and climate damage.

"We are seeing a striking contrast," said Burck. "Progress on climate action is often slow and in some countries, such as the United States, things are even moving backwards. But technologically and economically there is enormous momentum."

That momentum is apparent in record solar energy growth. Last year 75% of global electricity demand growth was met by the green energy source, according to energy think tank Ember's latest global electricity review. Investment in clean energy has also outpaced that in fossil fuels for multiple years.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The rapid expansion of renewable technology, as well as the Iran War and a reduction in deforestation are behind a projected slight fall in emissions for the first time since the COVID-19 pandemic, according to the CCPI.

"Governments have to act now to turn the momentum into sustained emissions reductions," said CCPI co-author Niklas Höhne of the NewClimate Institute, which compiles the report with environmental NGO Germanwatch.

Burck attributed Germany's worst ever performance in the category of national climate policy to current policies being pursued by Germany's economy minister Katherina Reiche.

"Measures that primarily aim to increase the use of natural gas, threaten to undermine progress in the energy transition and risk significantly worsening the conditions for renewable energy and electrification for many years to come," said Burck.

A European Commission report published on November 9 on the sidelines of the UN COP31 climate summit in Turkey said Germany was one of nine EU countries set to miss 2030 emissions reductions targets.

Germany is not alone in its disappointing ranking. The other G20 countries — the world's leading industrialized and emerging economies, responsible for around 80% of global CO2 emissions — also perform poorly.

The only exception among them is the United Kingdom, which ranks seventh and received a high rating, performing well in greenhouse gas emissions, energy use and climate policy. However, study authors rated it low for renewable energy expansion.

The G20's oil- and gas-producing countries occupy some of the lowest positions on the climate action table. The United States, which is the world's second largest emitter, languishes alongside Russia, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Canada around the bottom of the league, with an overall rating of "very low."

The hosts of this year's COP31, also received a "low" overall score. Australia, a major coal exporter with some of the world's highest per-capita emissions, ranks 54th, while Turkey, which is also heavily dependent on fossil fuels, comes in 53rd.

China is the world's largest emitter of greenhouse gases and ranks 56th in the CCPI, receiving an overall rating of "very low." Its main weaknesses include its now high per-capita emissions and substantial energy consumption.

However, among the G20, China leads the way in renewable energy expansion. The country, which is five years ahead of schedule in reaching its goal of adding 1,200 GW of wind and solar capacity to the grid by 2030, also produces over 80% of the world's solar panels.

Several oil-producing countries, including Kazakhstan, Saudi Arabia, Uzbekistan and the United Arab Emirates, are also performing better than expected in the renewables category and "are significantly expanding their previously limited" capacity, said the report.

The authors said these countries have significant potential to further expand renewables.

"In the Arab states in particular, very high per-capita emissions and an above-average level of electrification coincide with a relatively low existing share of renewable energy and enormous solar potential," said co-author Natalie Pelekh in a statement. "These are, in fact, ideal conditions for more ambitious climate action."

This article was originally published in German.

#1018. Man Utd show fight on night of chaos to give Carrick a glimpse of hope

So maybe there is some fight left in the old dog yet?

At half-time, Manchester United looked down and out and Michael Carrick’s reign as manager as good as finished.

Roma were 2-0 in front and coasting, gorging on a desperate United’s litany of errors, and there was full-scale mutiny in the stands at Old Trafford. A fifth defeat in six matches and the club’s longest winless run for 48 years beckoned. It was toxic on and off the pitch.

And then something changed. United, from being a dishevelled, disorganised mess, suddenly seemed to remember who they were supposed to be and what they were supposed to represent. Surrender gave way to fight. A team that had been feeling sorry for themselves discovered some pride. A crowd that had been baying for blood turned Old Trafford into a bear pit of a very different kind, and Roma simply did not know what had hit them.

This club have served up some famous comebacks over the decades, but it was hard to think of too many occasions when the mood and momentum had shifted this violently from one half to the next.

United fans were in open revolt in that first half, releasing green and gold balloons in protests before kick-off and then throwing tennis balls on to the pitch amid furious chanting against the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe. The players looked like they would rather have been anywhere else.

And yet by the 86th minute Matheus Cunha’s wild celebrations were encapsulating a wild night, the Brazilian ripping off his shirt after his dramatic winner before launching himself into a delirious crowd drunk on the euphoria of a victory that had seemed improbable in the extreme at the interval, when boos cascaded from the stands.

Whether this proves little more than a thrilling, heroic interlude in the endgame for Carrick, or the start of a genuine turnaround, is hard to know. And, let’s be clear, there was so much about the first-half performance to concern the hierarchy, who came under persistent, furious attack from fans at war with an ownership it reviles and wants gone.

But the second half stood firmly at odds with the shambolic display that had preceded it and suggested all may not be quite lost just yet.

Aston Villa visit Old Trafford on Sunday in the final game before the international break and, if Carrick can follow this with another win, then it will be intriguing to see where the Old Trafford board goes from there.

Happy Tuesday and thanks for tuning in to tonight’s coverage of Manchester United against Roma.

It’s matchday four of the Champions League and Michael Carrick’s side host their Serie A opponents having failed to win any of their last nine matches across all competitions. Since their win against Sabah back in September (must feel like years ago to Carrick), they have suffered chastening defeats in Europe to Atlético Madrid and then Cesc Fabregas’s Como. This has been coupled with dismal performances in the Premier League, most recently a 2-0 defeat at the hands of Chelsea, where Lisandro Martínez was sent off for two ridiculous fouls.

Lisandro Martinez is shown a second yellow card following a VAR review 🟥 Watch live on TNT Sports and HBO Max ➡️https://t.co/WPrcA5ZrQ1 https://t.co/VLcAMNdqgZ

All in all, there is the feeling that Carrick is simply a dead man walking, limping towards the international break after the United hierarchy decided on a stay of execution in their crisis talks earlier this month. If the beleaguered manager has any hope at all of hanging on to his job, he needs convincing results tonight and against Aston Villa on the weekend.

Despite the doom-mongering that circles the club, Carrick maintains that he has buried the hatchet with Bruno Fernandes following his captain’s public criticisms of the club, insisting that “the dressing room is a good place” in his pre-match press conference (more on that to come).

The visitors on the other hand, managed by Gian Piero Gasperini – who replaced Claudio Ranieri last summer – are certainly having a better time of it. They got off to a slow start in Europe, drawing with Fernebahce in their opening match but coming agonisingly close to stunning Real Madrid on matchday two at home. They went 3-1 up before three late goals snatched victory for Madrid.

They bounced back with a convincing 4-0 win over Slovan Bratislava and their domestic campaign is off to an incredibly promising start. They are currently unbeaten in Serie A with seven wins and three draws. They sit third and are the highest scoring side, with 28 goals from their 10 games. Free-flowing though their attack is, there a certainly defensive frailties there to exploit as they conceded three in a six-goal thriller against Napoli, as well as two in both matches against Cagliari and Udinese.

It has been 19 years since Carrick was part of a United side that thrashed Roma 7-1 at Old Trafford, with the midfielder scoring two. Tonight he faces that same opponent with his job hanging by a thread and it remains to be seen if his team can produce any semblance of that spark to turn the tide. Feel free to drop us your score predictions in the comments – bragging rights on the line for the winner.

We’ll be bringing you team news, previews from the managers and more ahead of kick-off at 8pm!

#1015. DW Science explainer on the default mode network: what your brain does when you aren't focusing on anything, and why it's important.

Doing nothing might be the ultimate brain hack. When you're bored, the brain goes into default mode network. It's not only healthy for you, but it may also shape the very essence of your identity.

You know when you lock your phone and the screen goes black? It seems like it's not doing anything. But it's not doing nothing. It's syncing your messages, updating apps and running other background processes.

Imagine you're sitting on a bus, staring out of a window, taking a shower or walking, and you get that feeling of doing nothing and letting your mind drift?

Well, your mind, the brain, is doing a lot when it feels like you're doing nothing.

It's going over your memories, shaping your sense of who you are, imagining possible futures, helping you understand other people and connecting ideas.

That's your brain's default mode network.

Scientists conducted brain-imaging experiments in the 1990s and early 2000s to find out which regions of the brain were active during demanding tasks, like solving a math problem or memory exercise.

But to measure that, they needed a so-called baseline. They needed to know the level of brain activity at rest and during demanding tasks.

So, between the tasks, they asked participants to relax, close their eyes, stare at a fixed point on a wall, or try not to think of anything at all.

And they measured the participants' brain activity both when they were solving a task and doing nothing. That's how scientists noticed the brain was active in up- and downtime.

They noticed that when participants started to focus on a new task, after having done nothing, some brain areas lit up and other areas dimmed down. That suggests those areas that dimmed down must have been active while the participant was apparently — physically and mentally — at rest.

This realization eventually led to the discovery of the default mode network or DMN.

The DMN is crucial because it helps your brain make sense of your life and experiences.

It helps you connect and revisit memories, reflect on who you are, imagine what might happen in future scenarios, understand other people, build meaning from experience, and connect ideas in new ways.

It turns all your memories, experiences, knowledge, emotions and social information into your internal story. Think of that story as a constantly evolving, updated model of who you are and how you engage with the world around you.

But it's important to understand the DMN involves more than one area of the brain. It is a group of brain regions that light up when you're not focused on an external task.

There's another player in your brain that acts as a monitoring system. You can think of it as constantly asking "Is there anything that needs my attention?"

Imagine you're daydreaming while driving, and a car suddenly swerves into your lane.

In a fraction of a second, your daydream disappears and your attention snaps back to the road. That player is called the salience network, or SN.

The salience network helps you notice important signals, like a sound, a mistake, pain, an emotion, a threat, or something happening in your body, and helps shift the brain toward attention and control systems when action is needed.

The DMN, SN and attention/control systems constantly interact.

And the DMN doesn't just turn off completely with every hard task. Parts of it can also contribute when tasks involve memory, stories, meaning or other people.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Smartphones have filled many of the small empty moments of our days — waiting for the bus, standing in line, eating alone, lying on the couch. We are constantly looking at our devices.

So, it seems reasonable to ask: are we crowding out those moments of boredom where DMN kicks in?

Maybe. But so far, there's no strong evidence that scrolling directly affects mental health by reducing DMN time.

What we do know is that problematic smartphone use can increase stress, anxiety, task-switching and disrupt sleep.

And sleep loss and stress also have clearer evidence for altering DMN-related brain connectivity.

When your mind wanders, it might produce a great new idea.

But it might also replay an embarrassing thing you did five years ago. Again. And again.

In depression, the self-reflection part of the DMN can get caught in repetitive negative loops that are hard to stop — what's known as rumination.

Scientists have also found that Alzheimer's disease targets key DMN areas, particularly those responsible for your autobiographical memory and remembering other aspects of the past. Which may help explain why memory problems are so central to the disease.

Protect your sleep and take stress seriously. There is direct evidence that sleep loss and stress disrupt DMN-related connectivity.

Take real, quiet breaks after mentally demanding tasks, like studying. It can even help you memorize facts for your exam.

Try to reframe boredom as this essential, energy-intensive active work in your brain that builds your internal narrative and sense of self, consolidates memories, creates connections and sparks creativity.

Try waiting in line without checking your phone. Look out the window next time you take the bus or take a walk without listening to anything.

You can also try scheduling DMN time. It may be the closest thing to a real brain hack.

The fusion of club tradition with streetwear sensibility creates a capsule that feels equally at home on the terraces and the high street.

And while it was Mark Hughes who proved the hero in the 1991 final against Barcelona with both goals in a 2-1 victory, it was Bruno Fernandes who stepped up against Burnley â tucking away an injury-time penalty to secure another dramatic United win.

Whether in Europe more than three decades ago or in the Premier League today, the shirt seems to carry a touch of luck. Maybe United ought to start wearing it more often.

#1013. How to make climate anxiety your superpower

Late last week the UN’s climate conference, COP31, failed to reach a consensus on its headline message. That news came on the heels of the UN acknowledging that the 1.5 ˚C warming limit set out in Paris will be breached. So, it’s easy to feel anxious in a world where it seems that not enough is being done about climate change. But is it possible to overcome such anxiety or even use it?

In the final episode of Cooked? I open up about my own climate anxiety and discover that there are still things that I can do to battle climate change. And how those small individual actions could potentially lead to more systemic change.

00:00 Can I do anything about my climate anxiety?

04:43 What the science says about ‘ecoanxiety’

11:35 Can individuals really do anything?

Net zero emissions won’t reverse climate change — some nations look to ‘net negative’

The rise of eco-anxiety: scientists wake up to the mental-health toll of climate change

This episode was written and produced by Nick Petrić Howe. Dan Fox was the editor. Music was by Akio Jefferson, Jonathan Maiocco, Aerial Circles, and Lionel Cohen, and was provided by Triple Scoop Music via Getty Images. Thanks to Emma Lawrance, Kimberly Nicholas, Madalina Vlasceanu and Elizabeth Howe for featuring in this episode.

Nick Petrić Howe: Hi mum, can you hear me okay?

Nick Petrić Howe: If you’ve been listening to this series, you’ll know that I’ve been struggling a bit with anxiety about the climate. If you’re just joining us now, hi, I’m Nick Petrić Howe and I have a climate anxiety problem. Throughout this series, I’ve spoken to a lot of scientists about the big ideas and big data that we can use to tackle climate change, but I haven’t really addressed the core reason of why I wanted to do this — to figure out what to do with my own feelings about climate change.

I wanted to know if I’d always felt this way, and if so, what I could do about it. So, I called up an expert on me. My mum.

Nick Petrić Howe: Can I record this call for work?

Elizabeth Howe: Yeah, course you can yeah

Nick Petrić Howe: Yeah? I just wanted to ask you something. When I was a kid, was I an anxious worried child would you say?

Nick Petrić Howe: This wasn’t exactly what I was expecting. I feel like I worry about things and have worried about them a lot throughout my life. But maybe there was something special about climate change, I know that it’s held a special position in my life. It’s why I decided to study biology when I finished school, eventually doing a PhD — to figure out if there was some way to help save the planet. So, I tried a different tack.

Nick Petrić Howe: Do you ever remember me worrying about, like, the environment and stuff. Elizabeth Howe: Oh God yeah. You were always thinking about stuff like that.

Elizabeth Howe: Well because you said— there was a big thing about climate change and you said ‘oh well climate change isn’t real because, you see, what happens is, in science, is that the world has these ice ages and then everything melts and then daa daa daa daaa.’ So you said, ‘it’s just a normal event, it’s not anything to do with global warming and it’s a load of rubbish.’ But you were always looking into stuff like that and listening to stuff like that. You were very interested in the scientific explanations for things.

Nick Petrić Howe: I’m not sure how I feel about that to be honest.

Nick Petrić Howe: Not gonna lie, being outed as a junior climate denier was not on my bingo card for this year. We eventually came to the conclusion that this was a phase I went through when I was quite young and hadn’t quite understood that people could just well… lie on national television. Misinformation, unfortunately, isn’t just a new thing. When I was a kid in the 90s, there were campaigns to make climate research seem a lot more questionable than now, and established politicians like Lord Nigel Lawson in the UK openly criticised the science.

At least, it seemed, I was interested in the climate. For the record, now I absolutely am convinced, along with the scientific community, that climate change is real and human caused.

And, even according to my mum, as I got older, I cared more about the climate, even if I wasn’t necessarily worried.

Elizabeth Howe: I don’t think you were particularly too worried…

Nick Petrić Howe: In fact, I remember thinking when I was a teenager and I was more appraised of the actual facts, that climate change was a solvable problem. One that my generation could fix. I was filled with notions of all the things that science had accomplished — the moon landings, the internet, and general relativity — breakthroughs that solved problems once thought insurmountable. It took me getting older to become a bit more jaded, concerned that we’d not done enough soon enough and that maybe it was too late.

But this got me thinking, if I wasn’t worried once and even felt hopeful. Is that something I could recapture? This series has already taught me that in many ways we’ve done more than I thought to tackle climate change and that people are actively working on solutions. But that only goes so far to assuage my own anxiety. So you’ll forgive me if I spend this episode figuring out if there’s something that can help me. Is there anything I can do?

Nick Petrić Howe: As I said, I’ve struggled with anxiety about climate change. Sometimes I feel paralysed by how hopeless it all seems. There’s so much to do and it’s not getting done fast enough. At the same time, every other week there seems to be another climate record smashed or a natural disaster exacerbated by climate change.

It’s easy to feel anxious. So, in this third and final episode of Cooked? I wanted to know - am I normal? Or am I bit of an outlier here? Are other people having these feelings of hopelessness in the face of climate change.

So, I called up one of the world experts on how climate change is affecting mental health.

Nick Petrić Howe: This is Emma Lawrance, from Imperial College London. After figuring out our settings, we connected on a slightly better line. And Emma told me that I’m by no means alone, in fact, it turns out there is a name for what I’m feeling. There’s a few actually.

Emma Lawrance: So there is this kind of emerging plethora of terms really that all centre on this kind of umbrella of what we might call psychological responses or emotional responses to the climate crisis. And so some of those terms can be things like climate related distress, climate anxiety, eco anxiety, ecological grief, solastalgia.

Nick Petrić Howe: And while there are differences between these terms, for the purposes of the podcast I’m just going to say eco-anxiety — the anxiety about climate change and environmental destruction, as that seems the most fitting with my experience.

And one of the first things that Emma impressed upon me is that there’s a lot we don’t know about eco-anxiety. This is a rapidly emerging field, but eco-anxiety is a thing that a lot of people are feeling. Especially if they’re dealing with the consequences of climate change.

Emma Lawrance: So for instance, in our sample of nearly 3,000 young people surveyed across the US, one fifth of the young people who didn't report experiencing a climate change-related event were afraid to have children that rose to one third of the young people who said they had already experienced a climate change-related event. And there was a correlation between the people sort of self-reporting and looking at their postcodes and where you know, climate hazards had been in the US. So, they seem to be kind of reflecting sort of a real-world experience.

Nick Petrić Howe: And that makes sense. If climate change is affecting you, then you would worry about it. I know my own anxiety spiked during the heatwaves, wildfires and droughts of this last British summer. But that does also mean that there are certain people who worry a bit more than others.

Emma Lawrance: There's more and more studies showing that eco-anxiety is definitely not like a white Western phenomenon. This experience of distress and what can be called eco-anxiety in response to changing climate is actually much higher in the countries and in the communities where these impacts are already occurring.

Nick Petrić Howe: That might surprise you, it certainly did me - In some ways, I had thought that maybe this was a worry more for people like me. Western, relatively well-off folks, who have time to worry about things. But, if my anxiety spiked over one record breaking summer, perhaps it shouldn’t be shocking that people facing these impacts week after week in the developing countries most effected, but least responsible for climate change are worried too. And they’re only getting more worried.

Emma Lawrance: It's happening in ways that are then compounding. So people are experiencing not just one, but multiple kind of stresses and disasters, often coming back-to-back and they're not having time to recover before the next one hits that experience into place with this awareness of, well, what's to come? The awareness of the injustice of the situation of often kind of insufficient climate action and power dynamics between, you know, the people who are affected and the people causing the problem and growing inequalities in some spaces or many spaces globally. those things are we're seeing this really rapid increase in the use of the term eco anxiety. So I think there's over a 4,000-fold percent increase in Google searches. five-year period. And so, it’s really skyrocketed

Nick Petrić Howe: Strangely, it feels a little better to know that I’m not alone in these feelings. Perhaps I am a bit more normal than I thought. But I wanted to know what could be done about these feelings. For me, the anxiety has sometimes been paralysing. I haven’t wanted to engage with climate news, which, as I’ve said, is a bit of a funny position to be in as a science journalist. And Emma explained to me that, for some people it can be like that. It can even affect people’s daily lives, and those people may need some extra help and support, but for many people this anxiety can be quite an understandable reaction.

Emma Lawrance: Eco-anxiety isn't something that the vast majority of researchers and people living with these experiences and profession and, mental health professionals would say needs to be a quote unquote, like diagnosis. And it's something that is, can be very rational. It's understandable, and often proportionate to feel alarm, to feel distressed, to feel the strong emotions in response to the facts of the climate crisis.

Nick Petrić Howe: And for some people, it may even be a feeling they want to hold onto. They can use it to push them to battle climate change.

Emma Lawrance: We also know that people who are feeling that distress are more likely to be taking pro-environmental action. We know that collective action, particularly rather than individual action can help you like hold high distress and protect your mental health and wellbeing. it's not sometimes holding distress can impact, you know, is related to poorer mental health, it's related to higher insomnia, et cetera. But young people are saying, you know, we don't want our distress to be taken away in a sense, because this shows that we care. It shows that we care about the world. It can be fuel for action, but that action needs to be often done with others. And also can for some people lead into action that ends up providing more meaning and joy and purpose and it can be a really good thing, but for others it can be overwhelming and paralysing and have really severe impacts on their life

Nick Petrić Howe: So, to my question of what I’m supposed to do with these feelings... I think I’m already doing it. These feelings can overwhelm, and I’ve certainly felt that. But maybe doing something is a way to help live with these anxious feelings. The question is though, what do you do?

Kimberly Nicholas: I really think if your listeners were taking these high-impact climate actions just 20 minutes a day. It would be enough.

Nick Petrić Howe: Now, what I don't want to do is make you feel as though the weight of the world is on your shoulders. Saying that you are ultimately responsible for climate change is too much of a burden for any one person to bear. As someone who worries a lot, I think that weight would crush me, frankly. It’s also fair to say that many of these problems are systemic too. Governments, nations, and businesses should all meet ambitious climate targets if we’re to avoid the worst consequences of climate change. And if you live in the US, say, even if you have very minimal emissions compared to your neighbours, you’re likely to have higher emissions than someone in Bangladesh — just because of how baked in carbon emissions are. If you have an electric car in the US, for example, it’s getting electricity from more fossil fuel power plants than someone in Norway. So, it’s easy to think that any individual action is a waste of time.

Kimberly Nicholas: Well, ineffective individual actions are a waste of time.

Nick Petrić Howe: This is Kimberly Nicholas, a climate scientist at Lund University. And she’s someone who’s spent quite a bit of time thinking about what individuals can do, and perhaps what they shouldn’t do.

Kimberly Nicholas: We don't need to focus on recycling or canvas bags. People really have the wrong ideas about what individual action means. And so that I think is a myth that we need to dispel. So, it's not about doing everything, it's not that every little thing matters, it's that focusing our limited time and energy where it can really make a difference can lead us to take powerful actions today that do lead to system change.

Nick Petrić Howe: And it’s not just the what that Kimberly has been thinking about, it’s the who too.

Kimberly Nicholas: I really focus on this group that is in the top 10% globally, many of whom are surprised to learn that they are in that group. So if you earn over about 38,000 US dollars or 35,000 euros a year, your income is in the top 10% globally. And that group produces about half of household carbon pollution and also has enormous political, economic, cultural power.

Nick Petrić Howe: I was among those surprised to find myself in that group. Being in the 10% of income doesn’t quite gel with my, admittedly comfortable, but fairly ordinary life. It’s worth saying as well, that power and carbon emissions track income as it rises too. With around a fifth of warming between 1990 and 2020 attributable to people in the top 1% of income, and a bit under a tenth to those in the top 0.1%.

But the top 10%, which I’m going to guess includes a lot of you listening, still have a lot that they can do, according to Kimberly. She notes that things like reducing air travel, investing in low-emission funds, and switching to renewable energy providers could be effective. She’s even created a guide for people online where you can find what the highest impact climate actions you personally can take. She calls it finding your superpower.

Now, there are researchers who are critical of these ideas. Arguing that individual actions, like these, are a distraction from larger more systemic changes that should be taking place. And others have argued that the fossil fuel industry has used individual actions to take onus off themselves. In fact, carbon footprints — which focus on the emissions of an individual — were popularised by the fossil fuel industry.

But I spoke to a lot of different experts for this series, and they mostly agreed on both being important. We’ll need individual actions and systemic changes. And one doesn’t preclude the other. Things like individual actions may also actually lead to bigger changes.

This is also why Kimberly focuses on specific actions that she feels will have the biggest impacts. And one key one for those who live in a liberal democracy, where you can freely vote for your leaders, is to try and use your individual power to lead to systemic change.

Kimberly Nicholas: For those of us who do live in those countries, we have incredible powers like voting and encouraging and getting others to vote, mobilizing voting, joining a political party or organization that's taking powerful climate action. And the reason those types of actions are so important is that climate policies that affect everyone in a society, of course, have enormous potential, far bigger than, you know, our everyday lives at home, to really move the needle and dramatically decrease climate pollution.

Nick Petrić Howe: And it’s not just politics. This could also be things like engaging with climate action at work. Many workplaces have climate goals and there are usually other keen people you can connect with to try and make these goals happen. Maybe your own climate efforts are small, but a company of 10, 100 or thousands of people could make a much more tangible difference.

For example, there has been an employee-led effort to urge their companies to leave the US Chamber of Commerce. This business association rejected the scientific consensus on climate change until 2019 and has historically obstructed climate action. More recently, it has acknowledged that humans contribute to climate change, however, it still lobbied against the Inflation Reduction Act. So, climate concerned employees of the companies that are members of the Chamber have been petitioning their firms to leave the organisation. Many of those companies have now objected to the Chamber’s climate policies.

In fact, when I spoke to Kimberly it seemed that a lot of the ‘individual’ actions she suggested were really about connecting to others, be that political organising or simply socialising with other climate-conscious people. Those actions could build to something more, but they could also help with the reason I started this podcast in the first place. Anxiety.

Kimberly Nicholas: We want to make climate action fun. It should be something we look forward to and enjoy doing. That's one of the best parts of our week. and we know that from research, doing things together in community helps prevent burnout, it can help reduce anxiety, it can help motivate us and keep us going. And we all have ups and downs. I mean, we've all had moments of despair working on the climate crisis is not an easy thing to do. but we've also had moments of incredible elation and connection and creativity and joy. So being able to be in community is really powerful.

Nick Petrić Howe: And it could be that by connecting people together, that could ultimately lead to societal change.

Madalina Vlasceanu: I think there's this positive feedback loop by which all of our individual level actions can lead to bigger collective actions. And then collective actions can then trigger system level changes. The system level changes can then make it easier for individuals to take additional individual level actions because they would ideally remove the barriers to action.

Nick Petrić Howe: I have to admit that after my chat with Kimberley, I certainly felt a bit more empowered, but I was still a bit sceptical about the power of individuals. It’s not that I think individuals can’t do anything, it’s just the scale of the challenge that makes me hesitate. Even if I am, or even everyone listening is, the most climate conscious warriors in the world, it probably wouldn’t be enough. Like Kimberley alluded to, those individuals actions need to build towards the systemic. We need to change society.

I was curious about what the research said about the connection between the individual and the systemic and importantly, how can we actually get these small actions to help battle the global problem of climate change. So, I called up Madalina Vlasceanu, a social scientist who’s thought a lot about this exact issue.

Madalina Vlasceanu: So in my work we think about what are some ways in which collective action can be triggered at the individual level and then spread and catalyzed around groups and then collectives and then eventually making some system level pro changes.

Nick Petrić Howe: In our chat, one of the things that Madalina impressed upon me is that, while she believes that individual actions can lead to collective ones and then to systemic change, there are barriers that we need to acknowledge. For example, if you think the transition to renewable energy, the big barrier there is that fossil fuels are hugely subsidised. According to the International Monetary Fund, in 2024 fossil fuel subsidies were around $725 billion worldwide. If the underpricing of environmental costs are taken into account, such as air pollution and their contribution to climate change, that number rises to $6.7 trillion. In either case, fossil fuels are being made cheaper than they should be, which is not ideal when we should be using less of them.

Madalina Vlasceanu: So, our energy system needs to change and this can only happen through laws, policies, regulations that reduce, for example, fossil fuel subsidies currently valued at trillions of dollars. And in order for this to happen, for these systemic regulations to be introduced and enforced, there needs to, of course, be massive awareness campaigns from the public. So the public can push in this direction and make this direction the normative direction. So there is a big component here of the transition that has to do with laws, but the laws will likely change as an effect of pressure from the public.

Nick Petrić Howe: In fact, one reason that these subsidies persist is due to perceived unpopularity of raising the prices of fossil fuels — even if a switch to renewables would be cheaper in the long term. You may well have seen how people react to increases in heating or petrol costs. So, for politicians to make such changes, they’d need to believe that the public is on their side. Which is actually a strange position to be in, as most people do think that climate change is a big problem.

Research and polls show that the majority of people worldwide support climate action. So why do policymakers need convincing? Well, the problem is that support on a poll doesn’t necessarily translate to action.

Madalina Vlasceanu: There is a big difference between being aware of the problem in principle and being aware of this problem viscerally at a level where you know it's affecting you personally. So we know people have an optimism bias. and even though intellectually they can conceptualize that, well, there is this problem, people are talking about it, scientists are in agreement, it is going to get worse. And we understand that. At the same time, two things can be true. And so what is also true is that people think, well, this is probably not gonna affect me, or at least not very soon. And this is the type of thing where it'll probably happen first somewhere really far away or to other people or sometime in the pretty distant future. So I'd rather spend today or the near future thinking about more immediate issues that I have to worry about.

Nick Petrić Howe: I can certainly relate to spending my time worrying about things other than climate change. So, how do you actually get people to act? Madalina’s research has revealed some clues. By testing different interventions on a sample of 30,000 US citizens, she and a team of researchers were able to see what could actually get people to collectively act on climate change.

Madalina Vlasceanu: The top intervention leveraged two processes. So the two processes are efficacy beliefs and positive emotions. So efficacy beliefs means the belief that engaging in this activity will actually pay off in the exact way in which you're hoping it will. So the belief that if I do attend this protest, this protest will then reduce the risk of climate change. And so the way in which you can achieve this efficacy belief induction is by giving people examples of times in which such participation in collective action has actually had meaningful effects.

Nick Petrić Howe: Such examples include the banning of fossil fuel extraction in Quebec due to decades of grassroots movements and Los Angeles moving to ban urban oil extraction, because of years of protests and community organising.

Madalina Vlasceanu: And the other process I mentioned is positive emotions. So in addition to feeling like you will make a difference, you also need to feel like there is an emotional benefit to you personally, not just to the cause of the participation. So meaning-making, increasing belonging, or starting some close relationships with like-minded others. All of these more personal motivations to engage in collective action are also critical to engagement.

Nick Petrić Howe: Madalina also found that appealing to ideas like preserving the purity of the environment and respect for authority can also encourage more action — and these interventions were effective across the political spectrum.

To encourage more action, these interventions could be employed by governments, NGOs, charities and people making podcasts... They could say that you can make a difference, and you may even make some friends along the way. And by encouraging people to get together and act on climate, Madalina thinks we can create a positive feedback loop where more climate action is done, which makes it easier for us all to do more climate action.

Madalina Vlasceanu: It could be, for example, that someone's very motivated to not pollute very much or not use a lot of fossil fuels, but the system doesn't necessarily facilitate these actions. So it makes it much harder for me as an individual not to pollute, even if I wanted to. And so if I participate in collective action to change some of those systemic level decisions then it could be even easier for me to engage in individual level climate action by having an easier time engaging in in individual level behavioural change, such as you know, engaging in ways of transport that are less polluting.

If you’re sceptical about the power of groups of people, then we can take lessons from historical changes of the past. During the civil rights movement in the US, collections of small groups came together and organised protests, civil disobedience and boycotts that eventually led to new civil rights laws and the end of most legal discrimation against African Americans.

Madalina Vlasceanu: the main thing an individual can do to address climate change is to be less of an individual. And so we have to recognize the power in groups in the power of our collective to making change.

Nick Petrić Howe: So, if you want to fight climate change. Remember this. You can make a change, people have done it before, and it may even be good for you to do so.

Madalina Vlasceanu: Hopelessness is pretty natural, I would say. I felt hopelessness quite a lot at the beginning of this journey when I was first becoming aware of just how big the threat is. especially when I became a mother and I understood that my kids will inherit a very different world and a much worse one. Than I had. And so hopelessness is there. the one way I found to cope or to get out of it is by taking action. So action is the antidote to hopelessness.

Nick Petrić Howe: In this podcast series, I wanted to find out if there was anything I could do about climate change. And it turns out that perhaps things are not as bad as I thought. There are certainly challenges, and some big unknowns as to what might happen in the future.

But as humans, we have a tendency to focus on the negative. And when it comes to climate change, there’s plenty of negative to think about. Even if things are not as bad as I thought, we’re not really on track to meet our climate targets. We need more action, but perhaps that’s something in which we all have a role to play.

And according to the science, we can make a difference. I’m certainly trying to. [Since starting this podcast, I’ve changed my pension to be invested in climate-conscious way, joined a group organising for climate action in my company, and started talking more to people about climate. I’m talking to you right now. And that’s helped, with my anxiety. I just hope that it helps with the world.]

In the end, I turned my climate anxiety, into what I hope is a climate superpower — I’m still anxious but I’m using that energy to push me, to try and make difference. As Madalina said, Action is the antidote to hopelessness. I hope I’ve helped you feel a bit less hopeless.

For now, I’ll leave you with a final quote from Madalina.

Nick Petrić Howe: And then my last question is: how do we save the world?

Madalina Vlasceanu: Haha, good question. In my mind how we save the world is caring about each other and helping each other out.

Nick Petrić Howe: This podcast series was written and produced by me, Nick Petrić Howe. Dan Fox was my editor. Thanks also to Emma Lawrance, Kimberly Nicholas, Madalina Vlasceanu, and, of course, my mum for talking to me for this episode. And thank you all for listening too. If you like this sort of thing, then Kimberly has got her own climate podcast, I’ll link to that in the show notes as well.

#1011. Meet the world's most famous pub team: How a Sex Pistol, Superman and Vinnie Jones took Hollywood United  beyond Sunset Boulevard via private jet - and even rubbed shoulders with David Beckham's LA Galaxy

Published: 09:00 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 12:29 EST, 24 November 2026

They had a World Cup winner in defence, Superman in their squad and a Sex Pistol in charge of recruitment.

There's a clue in the name, but Hollywood United must have been the wildest, most star-studded pub football team of all time.

Ray Winstone, Jason Statham, Mike Myers and Vinnie Jones all turned out for a team that grew out of a gathering of British expats at the Cat & Fiddle pub in the late Eighties.

It being Hollywood, they travelled to matches by private jet and they even took on David Beckham in a charity match.

Now, as the Sex Pistols prepare to embark on a tour marking the 50th anniversary of their debut single, guitarist Steve Jones has revealed how he assembled the extraordinary side on Hollywood's Sunset Boulevard.

Among those who pulled on the shirt were France's World Cup-winning defender Frank Leboeuf, former Scotland captain Richard Gough and Brandon Routh, the American actor who played the superhero in the 2006 film Superman Returns.

Routh was given no special treatment by his team-mates, who would mockingly shout ‘Superman!’ whenever he made a mistake.

Hollywood United is the world's most famous pub team - featuring a littany of high-profile stars

Created by British expat and Sex Pistols star Steve Jones (right), United have rubbed shoulders with the likes of David Beckham

Vinnie Jones, meanwhile, had apparently lost none of the competitive instincts that characterised his career in English football.

In 2002, it was reported that he had been sent off just 15 seconds after coming on as a substitute in a Hollywood United friendly.

Anthony LaPaglia, the Australian actor who starred in the hit television series Without a Trace, was their goalkeeper.

There were members of the Sex Pistols, The Cult and Def Leppard, as well as actors such as Ralf Little.

But there were also rather less celebrated footballers.

‘The start of it was with me and Anthony LaPaglia; he was a goalie, and from there it turned into Hollywood United,’ Jones told the Telegraph.

‘We always used to play in a league with a bunch of regular blokes, carpenters and so on, then we got a few more faces who wanted to start kicking about with us like Vinnie Jones.’

The two Joneses met in a video shop in Los Angeles and the former Wimbledon hardman, who had embarked on a film career with Lock, Stock and Two Smoking Barrels, needed little persuasion to join.

‘He was up for a laugh, and he knows where to put a ball. Most of the team were amateurs, but we were decent and reached a certain level.’

In November 2007, Hollywood United took on Beckham's LA Galaxy in a charity match.

England manager Steve McClaren had flown to California to assess Beckham's fitness ahead of a European Championship qualifier against Croatia. It's not clear whether he attended the match, which Hollywood United lost 12-4. Beckham scored twice, as did Leboeuf and over 5,000 spectators raised more than $100,000 for victims of the California wildfires.

Steve Jones, now 71, had himself broken one of football's golden rules by changing his allegiance.

Vinnie Jones (left) and Ray Winstone (right) have turned out for the amateur football team

Actor Anthony LaPaglia lets the team travel on his private jet to matches across America

Having followed QPR as a schoolboy in west London and also been associated with Fulham, he became a Chelsea supporter after moving to California and getting sober.

Chelsea's games were available on American television and his lifelong friend and fellow Sex Pistol Paul Cook was already a diehard Blues fan.

Hollywood United played at Griffith Park, beneath the famous Hollywood sign, but their adventures would take them considerably further afield.

LaPaglia would arrange private jets to transport the players to matches.

Gough recalls one trip when the team flew to Vancouver for a charity match before heading straight to the Mexican resort of Puerto Vallarta to play a side of former Mexico internationals.

Vinnie Jones also told the Guardian in 2007 that Hollywood United had fielded nine former international footballers in a single match.

The club's ranks included former Liverpool and Newcastle defender Barry Venison and United States internationals Alexi Lalas and Eric Wynalda.

Winstone, a lifelong West Ham fan, found playing in the Californian heat rather more demanding than he had anticipated.

He later recalled being so exhausted by the time the ball reached him that he was barely able to kick it. And he wasn't particularly impressed by the willingness of former Chelsea defender Leboeuf to pass the ball, describing the Frenchman as a greedy player.

Among those watching from the touchline was the actor John Hurt, who was in town filming Indiana Jones and the Kingdom of the Crystal Skull with Winstone.

Some of the rock stars had impressive footballing pedigrees.

Ian Astbury, the lead singer of The Cult, had played boys' club football in Glasgow alongside future Everton and Scotland striker Graeme Sharp.

Gough, meanwhile, struck up a conversation with a team-mate from Northern Ireland without having the slightest idea he was Vivian Campbell, the guitarist of Def Leppard.

Sex Pistol Jones, who has lived in Los Angeles for more than 40 years, is returning to Britain next month for a tour marking the 50th anniversary of the release of Anarchy in the UK.

He still regularly attends football matches whenever he is back in England, although he has little time for the corporate hospitality enjoyed by many of his celebrity contemporaries.

‘I don't care where I sit, but I'm not interested in sitting in some box with a bunch of t***ers.’

#1003. Can global leaders put their money where their mouth is on climate?

World leaders warn that geopolitical divisions are distracting from the climate crisis as negotiations focus on clean energy and financing, while Iran calls for compensation for war-related environmental damage.

The slow international response to climate change has placed the world on a path to destruction, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres told heads of state and government during opening statements at this year's COP31 climate conference.

"The ⁠brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us," he said, as world leaders gathered in the Turkish resort city of Antalya to set the tone for negotiations at the UN climate summit.

A UN reportlast month found ​the world will cross a temperature threshold countries agreed to pursue in order to prevent runaway global heating. At the same time, states like Germany are slipping down the rankings for climate action, according to the annual Climate Change Performance Index published Wednesday by New Climate Institute and Germanwatch.

Nonetheless, Guterres said the world has "the power to make sure the overshoot is a temporary breach."

Negotiators from close to 200 countries are meeting in Turkey at the end of a year characterized by extreme heat waves and a glacier collapse in Nepal that triggered a flood, killing more than 1,400 people and leaving thousands more missing.

At this year's talks, national representatives are discussing climate solutions such as increasing the share of electricity in an effort to move away from fossil fuels.

On Thursday, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, one of the few heads of government from Europe's major economies attending the summit, said that the world's dependence on fossil fuels was at the heart of both the climate crisis and energy security challenges.

"The shift to clean energy is the only route to energy security," he said, endorsing the conference's focus on electrification which he said would lower energy bills, create jobs and protect people from the volatility of fossil fuel markets.

Burnham promised a "new era of British leadership over the next decade," announcing the UK would put climate resilience high on the agenda during its G20 presidency next year.

The US, the world's largest historical emitter of damaging greenhouse gases, is not attending the summit — for the second year in a row after US President Donald Trump withdrew the country from the Paris Agreement in 2025.

Other nations, including big polluters like Germany, France, Italy, Canada and Japan, also opted not to send their top leaders to the talks.

On Wednesday, Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, who is hosting COP31 together with Australia, which is leading negotiations, called on developed nations to take greater responsibility on climate finance.

Financing disagreements center around who should pay for international climate action, whether funding should take the form of grants or loans and how to scale monetary support for developing nations. Many of these countries are among the most vulnerable to the climate crisis but have contributed very little to the emissions causing it.

Erdogan said while previous conferences had resulted in different ideas around financing, they have yet to be turned into action. "We set out to make this an implementation COP," he told leaders.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen addressed remarks that developed nations are not contributing enough to climate finance, saying that the transition away from fossil fuels is in "our common interest."

"Europe is the world's largest provider of climate finance. Last year alone, we contributed more than €32 billion [about $35.5 billion] to support developing countries," she said, adding that Europe will continue to support partners worldwide in tackling climate change.

A recent Carbon Brief analysis found that public funding pledged under the Paris Agreement to help developing countries tackle climate change fell by more than 70% in 2026.

Most multi-year pledges from donor countries expired in 2025. Since then, the US has stepped back from international climate efforts, while several European countries have cut their aid budgets, reported Carbon Brief.

Hilda Heine, president of the Marshall Islands in the Pacific, which face an existential threat from rising sea levels, said the response to overshoot "must be overwhelming" and quickly reversed otherwise "the world we know is over."

"Every fraction of a degree of warming brings more catastrophe," said Heine, adding that more warming makes it more difficult to adapt to living on a hotter planet, brings greater loss and damage from worsening weather extremes and greater financial need.

She called on leaders to triple climate finance by 2035 and make it easier for Small Island Developing States to access the money.

"We are told there is no money, but their spending on war grows; the greatest security threat we face remains underfunded. I appeal to you: Find money for life, not death. Replenish the climate funds," Heine said.

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese spoke of a "solemn responsibility to this and to future generations ​to act," adding that this is the critical decade.

Australia, the world's third-largest fossil fuel exporter, has vowed to promote the views of the "Pacific family" — small Pacific nations in the region such as Tuvalu or Fiji, where pre-COP meetings were held in October.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Albanese said it was crucial that climate cooperation delivered practical results — "unlocking investment in clean energy technologies, accelerating electrification, speeding up action for our oceans, unlocking climate finance for those who need it ​most."

As reasons to speed up electrification von der Leyen pointed to wildfires in Europe and floods in Nepal, as well as droughts stretching from Central America to Sudan, and to the disruption to energy supplies linked to the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz.

"The world is witnessing the cost of continuing with the status quo for our climate and our energy security," she said, adding that the European Union would double down on efforts to become climate neutral.

"Three-quarters ​of humanity live in countries that import fossil fuels, hostage to price shocks they did ​not create and cannot ‌control," UN Secretary-General Guterres said, adding that recent conflicts have made clear a shift to renewable energy would help improve energy security and the cost-of-living crisis.

Von der Leyen also expressed support for COP31's 35-by-35 electrification pledge. The pledge aims to increase electricity's share of final global energy use to 35% by 2035, with von der Leyen saying Europe would be the first "electro-powered" continent.

Heine of the Marshall Islands said electrification must must be strictly tied to renewable energy generation rather than fossil fuels, warning that continued oil, coal and gas extraction was a threat to her country's survival.

Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said his country wanted compensation for environmental damage caused by US and Israeli strikes, including oil leaks from attacks on tankers. The strikes began in February.

Iran, which is a major fossil fuel producer and has pushed back against strict language on phasing out oil and gas at previous COPs alongside other petrostates, has also struck tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.

Pezeshkian linked the issue to climate finance and said his country expected "responsibility in times of war, to document and assess the environmental damages caused by military aggressions and to develop compensation mechanisms."

Brazil's President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who hosted last year's COP in the Amazonian city of Belem, said the momentum for climate action had dropped off at the start of the year, partly due to the Iran war.

"We started talking more about weapons and tariffs than the survival ‌of future generations," he said.

He also warned that "climate agreements are the favorite targets of reactionary forces at COPs," and urged leaders to work together. Lula promised to protect the Amazon rainforest. "Brazil is back to defend the continuity of a healthy planet," he said.

This article was last updated on November 12 to reflect incoming statements from world leaders.
